title: What is MBB, and how do McKinsey, BCG and Bain differ?
description: What MBB means, what the three firms have in common, and the differences candidates notice in their interviews and cultures.
hook: MBB stands for McKinsey, BCG and Bain, the three best-known strategy consulting firms. They are more alike than different: all three hire through case interviews and personal experience questions, and they work on similar senior-level problems. The differences that matter most for you are in how they interview: McKinsey's cases are usually interviewer-led, BCG and Bain usually expect you to drive, and each uses different online assessments.
body:
What the three firms have in common

  • Senior-level strategy problems, such as growth, M&A and large transformations, alongside substantial operations and implementation work.
  • Very selective hiring, with case interviews at the centre and real weight on personal experience and fit questions.
  • Similar career paths and an up-or-out promotion model.
  • Recruiting from universities, business schools and experienced professionals.

How their interviews differ

FirmOnline stepCase stylePersonal questions
McKinseySolve, a game-based assessment, for many rolesUsually interviewer-ledA Personal Experience Interview in each round
BCGVaries by office; often the Casey online caseUsually candidate-ledA skills interview on your experience and motivation
BainAn online assessment before interviewsUsually candidate-ledFit and experience questions; a written case in some offices

McKinsey

The interviewer leads the case with a sequence of questions: a structure, then perhaps a chart, a calculation, a brainstorm and a recommendation. Each interview also includes a Personal Experience Interview, a deep conversation about one real moment in your life, and McKinsey's own interviewing page asks you to come prepared to discuss your examples in detail. Full McKinsey guide.

BCG

BCG's careers site describes a skills interview (your experience, skills and motivation), a case interview and, for client-facing roles, a team interview. Live cases are usually candidate-led. Many offices screen with the BCG Online Case, a chatbot called Casey, which leads you through the questions itself. Full BCG guide.

Bain

Bain's careers site describes a digital assessment followed by case interviews for consulting roles, and asks candidates to explain why they want to join Bain specifically. Cases are usually candidate-led, and some offices add a written case in the final round. Full Bain guide.

Interviewer-led versus candidate-led, on the same case

A supermarket chain's profit has fallen from $120M to $90M on flat revenue of $2.0B. (Illustrative numbers.)

Interviewer-led (McKinsey style). After your structure, the interviewer asks: "Transport costs were $250M and rose 10%. How much of the decline does that explain?" You answer that question: $250M × 10% = $25M. The profit decline is $120M − $90M = $30M, so transport explains $25M ÷ $30M ≈ 83% of it. Margin fell from $120M ÷ $2.0B = 6% to $90M ÷ $2.0B = 4.5%. Then you say what it means and wait for the next question.

Candidate-led (BCG and Bain style). Nobody hands you the transport question. You say revenue is flat, so the problem is on the cost side, and ask for a cost breakdown. When you spot the transport increase, you size it yourself and propose the next step: "Transport explains about $25M of the $30M. I'd like to understand why it rose, fuel prices or delivery routes, and then look at the remaining $5M."

The thinking is the same. What changes is who steers. Practise both, and read how to drive a case for the candidate-led version.

What a strong answer sounds like

"Transport costs went up, so that's probably a big part of it."
"Transport explains about 83% of the profit drop: $25M of $30M. Margin fell from 6% to 4.5%. So the priority is transport, and I'd check whether the rise is a market-wide fuel effect or something specific to our network."

The strong answer quantifies, draws the conclusion and moves the case forward, whichever firm you are in front of.

Culture

Each firm has a reputation, and plenty of stereotypes. BCG's careers site lists integrity, intellectual curiosity, creative thinking, a collaborative mindset and drive; Bain mentions intellectual curiosity, entrepreneurial drive and enthusiasm for challenges. Such lists overlap heavily. The most reliable way to understand the differences is to talk to people who work there, ideally in the office you would join, because culture often varies as much between offices and teams as between firms. How to network for consulting covers those conversations.

Common mistakes

  • Preparing only one case style. Candidates who practise only candidate-led cases ramble in McKinsey interviews; those who practise only interviewer-led cases wait to be told what to do at BCG and Bain.
  • Treating personal questions as a warm-up. At all three, your stories are assessed seriously. Prepare several real ones you can discuss in depth.
  • Memorising firm "scripts". Interviewers spot rehearsed answers quickly, especially when a follow-up question breaks them.

Should you apply to all three?

If you want strategy consulting, usually yes. Most of the preparation is shared: structuring, maths, chart reading, synthesis and strong personal stories. Add firm-specific practice on top: interviewer-led cases and PEI stories for McKinsey, candidate-led cases for BCG and Bain, Casey-style timed practice if your BCG office uses it, and a written case if your Bain office does. Always confirm the format in your invitation, since processes vary by office and year.

Practice

In the supermarket case, the interviewer says the remaining decline came from a 1-point rise in shrinkage (stock lost to theft and waste) as a share of revenue. Does that explain the rest?

Show the answer

1% of $2.0B is $20M, far more than the remaining $5M. So either the rise is smaller than a full point, or other costs fell and partly offset it. The right response is to say so and ask: "That would be $20M, more than the $5M gap, so something else must have improved. Could I see the other cost lines?"

Where to go next

Read how the Big Four compare, then decide whether to aim for MBB, the Big Four or both. To practise both case styles, try a full case from the casebook.
